reviews.scope: Knowing where tangent is undefined, used to identify poles
reviews.reason: Identifying every pole and every open branch presupposes knowing that tangent is the sine over cosine quotient and is undefined where cosine vanishes. The special values tan0 and tan45 are incidental, but the undefined-angle concept is necessary.

reviews.scope: Meaning of sin(t)/cos(t) for all real angles
reviews.reason: The target defines tangent as sin(t)/cos(t) over all real t, excluding cosine zeros. That requires general-angle sine and cosine, which come from the unit-circle coordinates. Right-triangle ratios cannot reach branches beyond acute angles, so every route depends on it.

reviews.scope: Deriving period pi and transferring the principal branch
reviews.reason: The reduction formulas sin(t+pi)=-sin t and cos(t+pi)=-cos t give the quotient period pi in this proof. Another route reads the period off the antipodal point on the unit circle, since both terminal sides lie on the same line with the same slope.
reviews.counterexample: Antipodal unit-circle points at t and t+pi share one line through the origin, so they have equal slope and equal tangent without citing the formulas.

reviews.scope: Strict monotonicity via the tangent difference quotient
reviews.reason: The sine-difference identity gives a clean symbolic proof of strict increase. Monotonicity can also be shown other ways, such as increasing positive sine over decreasing positive cosine on [0,pi/2) combined with odd symmetry.
reviews.counterexample: On [0,pi/2), sine increases and cosine decreases while both stay positive, so their quotient increases. Odd symmetry then extends this to the full principal branch.

reviews.scope: Sign argument making the tangent difference positive
reviews.reason: Quadrant sign rules make the denominator cos(u)cos(v) and the numerator sin(v-u) positive in this proof. Those signs can also be read directly from unit-circle coordinates or the graphs, without studying the sign rules as a separate topic.
reviews.counterexample: A student can see from the unit-circle coordinates or the cosine graph that cosine is positive on (-pi/2,pi/2), without memorizing quadrant sign tables.
